title: System Call
body:
How a user-mode program asks the [[Kernel]] to do something it is not allowed to do itself:
read a file, write to the screen, allocate memory, start a process. The only legal way
across the privilege boundary.

## It is not a function call

That is the whole point. A `jsr` transfers control but changes nothing about privilege, so
jumping into kernel code from user mode would either fail on the first privileged
instruction or, if it worked, mean there was no protection at all. A system call is a
**deliberate exception**: the program executes a trap instruction, the hardware switches to
[[Supervisor State]], saves the [[Status Register]] and PC, and vectors to a fixed handler
address the kernel installed. The kernel decides what to do; `rte` returns and drops
privilege back.

On the 68000 the instruction is `trap #n`, and on the Atari ST the OS entry points are
exactly that: `trap #1` for GEMDOS, `trap #13` and `trap #14` for BIOS and XBIOS. You push
the arguments and a function number on the stack, execute the trap, and clean up after.

```
    move.w  #$0009,-(sp)     ; function 9 = print line
    pea     msg
    trap    #1               ; into the OS
    addq.l  #6,sp            ; caller cleans the stack
```

The consequences worth carrying forward:

- **The kernel chooses the entry point, not the caller.** The vector table is set up in
  supervisor mode, so user code can only arrive where the kernel decided it may arrive, and
  with the arguments it agreed to accept.
- **It is expensive.** A mode switch, register saves, argument validation, then all of it
  again on the way back. Which is why buffered I/O exists: one system call moving 4KB beats
  4096 calls moving a byte.
- **`printf` is not a system call.** It is library code that eventually makes one. The C
  library you used in [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] is a wrapper around this
  mechanism, which is why it never looked like anything special.

Same hardware path as an [[Interrupts|interrupt]], different trigger: an interrupt is
asynchronous and comes from a device, a trap is synchronous and the program asked for it.
